title: Water filters: what they remove
summary: Shows what carbon, reverse osmosis, UV, ceramic, hollow-fibre and KDF filters do and do not remove, and what the NSF/ANSI marks mean. Most home filters do not remove germs, so the water still needs boiling or disinfecting unless the filter is certified for microbes.

steps.text: Treat water as unsafe until it has been filtered and disinfected, unless it comes from a source you trust.
Read the filter’s label and data sheet for an NSF/ANSI mark, and read exactly what it claims to remove.
Settle or filter cloudy water first, then boil or disinfect it.
steps.warn: A filter past its rated life can release what it caught. A filter with no date or label counts as spent.

notes:
## The rule first
- Most pitcher, fridge, faucet and under-sink filters are made for taste and chemicals. They are **not designed to remove germs** (CDC).
- Unless the label shows a microbe certification, boil or disinfect the water anyway.
- Boil at a rolling boil for 1 minute. Above 2,000 m (6,500 ft), boil for at least 2 minutes (Health Canada BWA).
- Boiling and bleach do **not** make water safe if it holds fuel, toxic chemicals or radioactive material (CDC).

## What each type does
| Type | Does | Does not |
|---|---|---|
| Granular carbon (GAC) | Chlorine taste and odour. Some organic chemicals. Certified units can cut PFOA and PFOS (EPA). | Bacteria, viruses, nitrate, fluoride, hardness, most metal ions (UGA, UNL). Neglected carbon can grow bacteria (UGA, UNL). |
| Carbon block | Same job, packed tighter. Can catch some Giardia and Cryptosporidium cysts (UGA). | Bacteria and viruses. Clogs easily. Trust cyst removal only with an NSF/ANSI 53 or 58 cyst claim (CDC). |
| Reverse osmosis (RO) | Many dissolved chemicals, such as lead, copper, arsenic and fluoride. CDC also lists RO as removing germs, including viruses. | Not every chemical (EPA). A typical unit wastes at least 5 gal for each 1 gal made (EPA). Makers don't count on it for germs: Pentair says to disinfect before or after its unit, and DuPont doesn't guarantee its membrane removes cysts and pathogens (Pentair RO-2550, DuPont TW30). Boil what a salvaged or home unit makes. |
| UV lamp | Inactivates bacteria, viruses and protozoa in clear water (WQA). | Chemicals and metals (EPA). Nova Scotia wants water under 1.0 NTU turbidity for UV, and says to filter it through a 10 micron or finer filter first (Nova Scotia UV). |
| Ceramic | Depends on pore size. Absolute 1 µm or less: parasites. Absolute 0.3 µm or less: bacteria too (CDC). | Viruses (CDC). A "nominal" or "mean" size may miss germs (CDC). |
| Hollow fibre | Sawyer's 0.1 µm absolute filter is rated for bacteria and protozoa. Ultrafilters with 0.01 µm pores should stop viruses (CDC Yellow Book). | Viruses, unless the pore size is 0.01 µm (CDC Yellow Book). |
| KDF | Copper-zinc media. Maker says it cuts chlorine and water-soluble heavy metals (Kymera). | Not a germ filter. Maker lists NSF/ANSI 42 (taste and odour) only. Usually paired with carbon. |

## What the marks mean
| Mark | Meaning |
|---|---|
| NSF/ANSI 42 | Taste and "aesthetic" claims: chlorine, odour, particles, iron, zinc and more (NSF). |
| NSF/ANSI 53 | Health claims, over 50 of them: lead, cysts, VOCs, chromium (NSF). "Cyst reduction" means parasites only (CDC). |
| NSF/ANSI 58 | Reverse osmosis systems (UL). Can carry cyst claims (CDC). |
| NSF/ANSI 401 | Up to 15 trace "emerging" compounds: drugs, herbicides, pesticides (NSF). |
| NSF/ANSI 55 | UV systems. Class A, 40 mJ/cm²: water of unknown quality. Class B, 16 mJ/cm²: extra treatment of water already judged acceptable (WQA). |
| NSF/ANSI 244 | Extra microbe filter for water that is already safe. Covers the gap between a contamination and a boil-water notice (WWD). |
| NSF P231 | Purifier: 6-log bacteria, 4-log virus, 3-log cyst. For water of unknown quality that is presumed drinkable, not sewage (WaterWorld, UL). |

A mark covers only the claims on the performance data sheet. Read the exact claim. For lead, look for NSF/ANSI 53 lead reduction, plus NSF/ANSI 42 particulate Class I (EPA). Only P231 and UV Class A are built for water of unknown germ quality. Even then, boil if you can.

## Typical rated capacity
- Brita standard pitcher filter: 40 gal (151 L), about 2 months (Brita).
- Brita Elite (Longlast): 120 gal (454 L), about 6 months. No more than 2 gal (7.5 L) a day. Water 0 to 29 °C (Brita).
- GE MWF fridge filter: rated 170 or 300 gal. Replace every 6 months, at rated capacity, or sooner if flow drops. Use it on water at 0.6 to 38 °C (33 to 100 °F), and drain it before it can freeze (GE).
- Keurig coffee-maker water filter: every 2 months (Keurig).
- Past its life, a carbon filter can fill up and release the organic chemicals it caught (UGA).
- A filter with no label or date: treat it as spent.

## Salvage angle
- **Fridge filters:** sealed, in-date cartridges are the prize. Used ones are spent.
- **Pitcher and faucet filters:** keep the housing and seals. Fit a fresh cartridge. Check the data sheet for lead (53) and Class I particles (42) (EPA).
- **Under-sink RO units:** pre-filter housings, tank, membrane housing, tubing and fittings. Plan for the reject water (EPA). Disinfect the water a salvaged unit makes (Pentair RO-2550).
- **Aquarium UV sterilisers:** not for drinking water. Fluval's UV-C steriliser manual says not to use it with drinkable liquids. The lamp gives UV-C, which harms eyes and skin. Trust a UV unit only with an NSF/ANSI 55 mark, and Class A for doubtful water.
- **Coffee-maker filters:** small cartridges that help remove impurities (Keurig). They make no germ claim, so do not count on them.

## If the water is doubtful
1. Let cloudy water settle or filter it, then pour off the clear water (CDC).
2. Boil it for 1 minute, at least 2 minutes above 2,000 m (6,500 ft) (Health Canada BWA). Boiling doesn't remove nitrate and can raise it (Health Canada BWA), so well water that may hold nitrate needs a test, or another source, before it goes into a baby's formula (AHS nitrate).
3. No fuel? Add unscented household bleach, 5 to 9 %: 2 drops per litre or 8 drops per gallon of clear water. Double it for cloudy or very cold water (CDC). Wait 30 minutes (CDC), or 1 to 2 hours, covered, if the water is cloudy or colder than 10 °C (50 °F) (HealthLinkBC 49b).
4. Most filters skip viruses. Filter first, then disinfect (CDC).

## Batch doses for buckets, drums and totes
These are for clear water: settle or filter cloudy water first. Use plain unscented bleach or plain calcium hypochlorite (pool shock), never stabilised pool chlorine with cyanuric (isocyanuric) acid in it (NSW Health).

| Water | Bleach, 5 to 9 % | Pool shock stock solution | Dry pool shock, 65 % |
|---|---|---|---|
| About 20 L (5 US gal) | 2.5 mL (½ tsp, about 40 drops) (CDC) | 200 mL* | Use the stock |
| About 200 L (a 55 US gal drum) | About 20 mL* | 2 L* | Use the stock |
| 1,000 L (an IBC tote) | About 100 mL* | 10 L* | 8 g (NSW Health), dissolved in a bucket of water first |

*Calculated: bleach at CDC's 0.1 mL (2 drops) per litre, stock at 1 part to 100 parts water (EPA). Health Canada's page counts 2 drops as 0.2 mL, double the 0.1 mL of CDC and HealthLinkBC 49b (Health Canada emergency); this table follows 0.1 mL. With 5 % bleach both come to about 5 mg/L, the tank dose in NSW Health's tables: 40 mL of 12.5 % sodium hypochlorite liquid or 8 g of 65 % calcium hypochlorite per 1,000 L (NSW Health). Healthy WA's first dose for a tank matches: 40 mL of 12 % liquid per 1,000 L, or 14 g of 60 to 70 % granules per 2,000 L (Healthy WA). Double every dose for cloudy or very cold water (CDC).

**Pool shock stock solution** (full method in [Chemicals](#ref/reference_chemicals/pool_chlorine_for_drinking_water)):
- Work outdoors or by an open window, with eye protection on. Pool shock is a very strong oxidiser (EPA).
- Keep pool shock sealed and dry, and away from gasoline, oil, paint solvents and oily rags. Never mix it with other chemicals: a little water or a mix-up can give heat, fire or toxic gas (EPA pool alert). Never mix bleach with ammonia, vinegar or other acids, or cleaners: [Chemicals](#ref/reference_chemicals/never_mix).
- Stir 1 heaping teaspoon, about 7 g (¼ oz), of plain granular calcium hypochlorite into 7.5 L (2 US gal) of water until it dissolves. That gives about 500 mg/L (EPA). Chlorine goes into the water, never water onto the chlorine (Healthy WA).
- Add 1 part stock to 100 parts of the water you are treating (EPA). Don't keep the stock (see [Chemicals](#ref/reference_chemicals/pool_chlorine_for_drinking_water)), and label the bucket so nobody drinks from it.

**Mixing and waiting**
- Stir well (CDC). In a drum or tote, use a long, clean paddle.
- Wait at least 30 minutes (CDC). The water should smell faintly of chlorine. If it doesn't, add the same dose again and wait 15 minutes more (EPA).
- Chlorine works best around 20 °C (68 °F). If the water is cloudy or colder than 10 °C (50 °F), double the dose and let it stand 1 to 2 hours, covered (HealthLinkBC 49b). Water from ice holes, snow and unheated tanks is often that cold.
- Chlorine fades in storage, by how long and how warm it is kept (Sphere). Test stored water again before you drink it.

**Check the residual**
- Smell is a rough check. A pool or spa kit that reads free chlorine (DPD) is better. For a batch you have just treated, aim for at least 0.5 mg/L free chlorine after at least 30 minutes at pH below 8 (WEDC Mobile Note 7, quoting WHO). MSF's cholera guidance wants 1 mg/L after 60 minutes if the pH is above 8 (MSF cholera). Sphere's 0.2 to 0.5 mg/L is the level it asks for at the point of delivery of chlorinated water (Sphere). How to test, and what to do with no reading: [Test drinking water](#guides/test_water).
- Old bleach gives a weak dose. EPA says to use bleach kept at room temperature for less than a year (EPA). Check old bleach first: [Test bleach strength](#guides/test_bleach_strength).
- Bleach doesn't kill Cryptosporidium (Washington DOH, Health Canada protozoa) and is generally not effective against Giardia (HealthLinkBC 10); lake and river water can carry both (HealthLinkBC 49b). For surface water, boil it or use a filter rated for cysts, then add chlorine if you want it protected in storage (Sphere).
